/-!
# Erdős Problem 729

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/729](https://www.erdosproblems.com/729)
- [EGRS75] Erdős, P. and Graham, R. L. and Ruzsa, I. Z. and Straus, E. G., *On the prime factors of $\binom{2n}{n}$*. Math. Comp. (1975), 83-92.
- [Er68c] Erdős, P., *Aufgabe 557*. Elemente Math. (1968), 111-113.
-/

namespace Erdos729

/--
Let $C>0$ be a constant. Are there infinitely many integers $a,b,n$ with $a+b> n+C\log n$ such
that the denominator of $$\frac{n!}{a!b!}$$contains only primes $\ll_C 1$?

Erdős [Er68c] proved that if $a!b!\mid n!$ then $a+b\leq n+O(\log n)$. This has been proved in the affirmative by Barreto and Leeham, using ChatGPT and Aristotle, with a modification of the argument used for [728].
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos729.lean"]
theorem erdos_729 :
    answer(True) ↔ ∀ (C : ℝ) (hC : C > 0),
      ∃ K ≥ 3, Set.Infinite { T : ℕ × ℕ × ℕ |
        let (a, b, n) := T
        a > 0 ∧ b > 0 ∧ n > 0 ∧
        (a : ℝ) + b > n + C * Real.log n ∧
        ∀ p, p.Prime → p > K →
          padicValNat p ((n.factorial / (a.factorial * b.factorial) : ℚ).den) = 0 } := by
  sorry

end Erdos729

reformulations.difference: EGRS75 asks for infinitely many n with suitable a,b, whereas Lean requires an infinite set of triples (a,b,n).
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Fix K and a bound N on n. Choose a prime p > max(K,N). For any admissible triple with n ≤ N, p does not divide n!. If p divided either a! or b!, it would therefore divide the reduced denominator, contradicting the condition at p > K. Consequently a,b < p, and n < p as well, so all such triples lie in a finite box. Infinitely many triples thus require infinitely many n. Conversely, a finite set of triples has a finite n-projection. This equivalence was proved independently in /workspace/review/equivalence.lean as triples_infinite_iff_n_infinite and incorporated into original_paper_rhs_iff; their axiom lists contain no sorryAx.

reformulations.difference: The source bounds the prime divisors of the reduced denominator by a constant depending on C. Lean instead uses a natural K ≥ 3 and requires padicValNat p denominator = 0 for every prime p > K.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Rat.den is always nonzero. For prime p and nonzero d, padicValNat p d = 0 is equivalent to p not dividing d. The Lean condition is therefore exactly that every prime divisor of the denominator is ≤ K. The extra lower bound K ≥ 3 is harmless: replace any natural bound K by max K 3. The quantifier position makes this bound uniform across the infinite family. The complete RHS equivalence with the direct prime-divisor formulation was proved in complete_rhs_iff in /workspace/review/equivalence.lean without using the sorried problem theorem.
